summary: Egypt's army museum fills Muhammad Ali's old harem palace: come as much for the 19th-century rooms as for the cannons.
look: In the Northern Enclosure of the Citadel, a long 19th-century palace with tanks, guns and a MiG-21 jet parked outside. Inside, hall after hall of weapons, uniforms and battle scenes, set in the rooms of Muhammad Ali's household palace.
story:
Muhammad Ali built the Haram, or Harem, Palaces in the Northern Enclosure in 1812 as private quarters for his household. The army museum was founded in 1937 in the old War Ministry building downtown, moved to a temporary home in Garden City, and came here in November 1949. It was renovated in 1982, 1993 and 2011.

The halls run from Ottoman and Muhammad Ali-era militaria through the wars of 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973 and the revolution of 1952. The 1973 war is covered only briefly, because a separate museum, the 6th of October Panorama, is devoted to it. If time is short, skip this one: the Citadel's mosques and view come first.
details: Outside: tanks, artillery and a MiG-21 jet fighter on display.
The Ottoman and Muhammad Ali militaria hall: swords, firearms and uniforms of the pasha's new army.
Look up and around: the rooms of Muhammad Ali's household palace are often more interesting than the displays.
fun_fact: The museum moved twice before settling in a harem: the private family quarters of the man who built Egypt's first modern conscript army.
narration: This long palace in the Northern Enclosure was built in 1812 for Muhammad Ali's household, the Harem Palace, and since 1949 it has housed Egypt's National Military Museum. Outside stand tanks, guns and a MiG-21 jet. Inside, the halls run from the swords and uniforms of the Ottoman and Muhammad Ali era to the wars of the 20th century. Fair warning: unless you love military history, the building is the main attraction, so walk through at your own pace and enjoy the palace rooms themselves. If time is short, skip it and spend the time on the view instead. Before you leave, take a look at the MiG parked outside.

summary: The palace that replaced the Citadel as Egypt's seat of power in 1874: 500 rooms, the royal home until 1952, and still a presidential palace.
look: A long European-style façade on Abdeen Square, in the 19th-century city west of the old town. Visitors see only the museums on the lower floors: arms, silver, the royal family, presidential gifts and historical documents. Security is strict: expect bag checks, have your passport with you, and ask before taking photographs.
story:
Khedive Ismail, Muhammad Ali's grandson, wanted a modern capital and a modern seat of government, away from the medieval Citadel. He built on the site of a small mansion belonging to one Abdeen Bey, whose name the palace keeps. Work began in 1863 and the palace was inaugurated in 1874. The French architect Léon Rousseau designed it with a crowd of Egyptian, Italian and French decorators. It cost 700,000 Egyptian pounds to build and two million more to furnish, and it has about 500 rooms. Joseph Urban added a wing in 1891, and Fuad I a garden in 1921.

From 1874 until the revolution of 1952 it was the main official residence of the royal family. Its most dramatic day was 4 February 1942, when British tanks surrounded the palace and the ambassador, Sir Miles Lampson, forced King Farouk to appoint Mustafa el-Nahhas as prime minister. Since 1952 it has been one of the presidential palaces, and the upper floors are kept for visiting dignitaries.

The Historical Documents Museum, opened in 2005, holds the Ottoman firman that made Egypt hereditary in Muhammad Ali's family.
details: The Arms, Silver, Royal Family and Presidential Gifts museums fill the lower floors; allow about an hour.
The Historical Documents Museum (2005): the Ottoman firman that founded Muhammad Ali's dynasty.
Look out for the clocks: the palace is full of them, most decorated with gold.
Abdeen Square in front: where British tanks drew up on 4 February 1942.
fun_fact: The documents include a certificate of the Order of the Iron Crown from the Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia, a short-lived South American kingdom almost nobody has heard of.
narration: Abdeen Palace marks the moment Egypt's rulers came down from the hill. For nearly 700 years they had governed from the Citadel. Then Khedive Ismail, Muhammad Ali's grandson, who wanted a modern, European-looking capital, built this palace on the site of a small mansion that belonged to one Abdeen Bey, and in 1874 moved the government here. It has about 500 rooms, a French architect, and cost 2.7 million Egyptian pounds with its furniture. Kings lived here until 1952. Its most dramatic day came on the 4th of February 1942, when British tanks surrounded the palace and the British ambassador forced King Farouk to appoint the prime minister Britain wanted. Today it is still a presidential palace, so security is tight and only the museums on the lower floors are open: arms, silver, the royal family and presidential gifts. As you walk through, look out for the clocks: the palace is full of them, most decorated with gold.

summary: Cairo's oldest mosque still in its original form: a vast brick courtyard of 879 and a minaret you climb by a stair that spirals round the outside.
look: About 2 km west of the Citadel, a huge square courtyard ringed by brick arcades on piers, with a domed fountain in the middle, all inside an outer enclosure. The minaret stands in that enclosure on the side away from Mecca, its stair winding round the outside. The Gayer-Anderson Museum adjoins the south-east corner.
story:
Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish officer who had spent his early career at the Abbasid capital of Samarra in Iraq, became governor of Egypt in 868 and soon ruled it as his own. He built this mosque in 876-879 as the centrepiece of his new city, al-Qata'i, in the Samarra style: brick piers, carved stucco and an outer enclosure. When the Abbasids razed the city in 905, they spared the mosque.

The minaret's date is debated. Some scholars credit it to Sultan Lajin, who hid in the ruined mosque after a sultan's murder, vowed to restore it, and did so in 1296. Next door, two 16th- and 17th-century houses form the Gayer-Anderson Museum, and parts of the Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me were shot at the mosque.
details: The minaret's outside spiral stair: the historian Ibn Duqmaq said it was wide enough for two camels.
Lajin's domed fountain of 1296 in the centre of the courtyard.
Under the ceiling: a wooden frieze of Kufic Quran text, nearly 2 km long in total.
The 128 stucco window grilles: a few of the simplest are original, the rest later.
fun_fact: Legend says Ibn Tulun was absent-mindedly twisting a strip of parchment round his finger in a meeting, and when asked what he was doing, said he was designing his minaret.
narration: If you have time for one detour, make it the mosque of Ibn Tulun, the oldest mosque in Cairo that still looks the way it was built, between 876 and 879. Ahmad ibn Tulun was a Turkish officer who had served the caliphs in Samarra, in Iraq, and he built in the Samarra style: brick piers, carved plaster and a huge open courtyard. When his city was burned in 905, only this mosque was spared. Legend says he designed the minaret by twisting a strip of parchment round his finger. Walk out to it and look at the staircase spiralling around the outside; if it is open, climb it for a wide view over the domes.

summary: A handful of words unlocks every building today: learn ablaq, muqarnas, iwan and sabil, and the façades start talking.
look: A glossary for the street. Start at the portal: a tall recess crowned by honeycomb muqarnas, often with striped ablaq stone around the arch. Then look up at the dome, which may be carved stone, and the minaret, usually built in three different tiers. Inside a madrasa, find the courtyard and its iwans.
story:
Ablaq is masonry in alternating courses of light and dark stone, as on the arch over Qalawun's entrance. Muqarnas are small niches stacked in tiers like honeycomb or stalactites; they carry portal hoods, minaret balconies and the corners of domes. By the late 13th century Mamluk portals had become tall recesses crowned with muqarnas, and Sultan Hassan's is the grandest. Mashrabiya is a lattice of small turned-wood pieces for windows and balconies: air in, eyes out.

An iwan is a hall open on one side to a courtyard; the four-iwan plan became standard for Mamluk madrasas. The qibla is the direction of Mecca, the mihrab the niche marking it, the minbar the stepped pulpit, and the dikka a platform for those who repeated the prayers to the crowd. A madrasa is a college, a khanqah a Sufi lodge, a sabil a charity fountain, a kuttab a Quran school, a wikala a merchants' inn, and a waqf the endowment that paid for it all.

From around 1400 domes were built of carved stone, first with zigzags, as on al-Mu'ayyad's mosque, then geometric and floral patterns, peaking under Qaytbay. Later Mamluk minarets usually had an octagonal first tier, a round second and a lantern with a bulb on top. The Ottomans brought pencil-shaped minarets.
details: Portals: a tall recess with a muqarnas hood. Sultan Hassan's is the grandest; Barquq's is a classic.
Ablaq: the striped stone of the arch over Qalawun's entrance.
Mashrabiya: the turned-wood screens at Bayt al-Suhaymi and on the Katkhuda kuttab.
Dome carving: zigzags on al-Mu'ayyad's dome by Bab Zuwayla; later domes carry stars and flowers.
Blazons: al-Ghuri's name in round medallions over the side iwan arches of his mosque.
fun_fact: Mamluk emirs put their old palace jobs on their coats of arms: a cup meant a former cupbearer, a pen box a secretary, crossed polo sticks the master of polo.
narration: Here is a pocket glossary for the buildings around you. Start at the door. Mamluk portals are tall recesses topped by muqarnas, little niches stacked in rows like honeycomb or stone stalactites. Around the arch you often see ablaq, bands of light and dark stone in alternation. On windows and balconies, the wooden lattices of small turned spindles are mashrabiya, letting the breeze in and keeping eyes out. Inside a madrasa, which is a college, the courtyard is usually framed by iwans, great halls open on one side. The biggest faces Mecca and holds the mihrab, the prayer niche, and beside it the minbar, the stepped pulpit. A khanqah is a lodge for Sufis, a sabil gives free water, a kuttab is a primary school, and a wikala is an inn for merchants. Now look up. From about 1400 domes were built in stone and carved, first with zigzags, later with stars and flowers. Minarets usually have three tiers of different shapes. Find the nearest dome and decide: zigzags or stars?
